title: Continuous images of compact sets
objectives: Prove that a continuous image of a compact set is compact.

screens.title: Where the image lands
screens.prose: Take $f(x) = xe^{-x}$ on a domain $[a, b]$ set by the sliders. The image $f([a, b])$ is drawn on the $y$ axis.

derive.caption: $f([a, b])$ = [{{fixed(min(a*exp(-a), b*exp(-b)), 4)}}, {{fixed(min(max(1, a), b)*exp(-min(max(1, a), b)), 4)}}]

screens.question: On $[0, 3]$, what is the largest value of $f$? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Read the top of the image segment.
$f'(x) = (1 - x)e^{-x}$ vanishes at $x = 1$.

byKey.end: $f(3) = 3e^{-3} \approx 0.1494$ is the right end, not the peak.
byKey.x: 1 is where the maximum occurs. The question asks for the value $f(1)$.

explain.text: $f$ rises to $f(1) = \tfrac1e \approx 0.3679$ and falls to $f(3) \approx 0.1494$. So $f([0, 3]) = [0, \tfrac1e]$, a closed bounded interval.

screens.title: Open domain, open end
screens.prose: Now use the open domain $(0, 3)$, which is not compact.
screens.question: What is $f((0, 3))$?

options.text: $(0, \tfrac1e]$: the top is reached at 1, but 0 is not reached
$[0, \tfrac1e]$, as before
options.why: $f(x) = 0$ only at $x = 0$, which is no longer in the domain.

options.text: $(0, \tfrac1e)$

hints.text: Which $x$ gives $f(x) = 0$?
Only $x = 0$, now removed.

feedback.correct: Right. The image is not closed.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check whether 0 and $\tfrac1e$ are reached.

explain.text: The image is $(0, \tfrac1e]$, which is not closed. A non-compact domain can lose an end of its image. Compactness of the domain is what keeps the ends.

screens.title: Images of compact sets are compact
screens.prose: Let $f : X \to Y$ be continuous and $K \subseteq X$ compact. We show $f(K)$ is compact. One line is tempting but flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\{V_\alpha\}$ be an open cover of $f(K)$.
Each $f^{-1}(V_\alpha)$ is open by continuity, and together they cover $K$.
$K$ is compact, so finitely many $f^{-1}(V_{\alpha_1}), \dots, f^{-1}(V_{\alpha_m})$ cover $K$.
Then $V_{\alpha_1}, \dots, V_{\alpha_m}$ cover $f(K)$, a finite subcover. $\blacksquare$
Take an open cover $\{U_\alpha\}$ of $K$; the images $f(U_\alpha)$ are open and cover $f(K)$.
lines.why: Images of open sets need not be open: $x^2$ maps $(-1, 1)$ onto $[0, 1)$ (l4). Pull covers back instead.

hints.text: Start with a cover of the image.
Pull back, take a finite subcover, push forward.

feedback.correct: Right. Pull back, choose finitely many, push forward.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Begin with an open cover of $f(K)$.

byKey.d1: You pushed open sets forward. Continuity only guarantees open preimages.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Preimages of the $V_\alpha$ are open and cover $K$. Finitely many suffice, and their $V$s cover $f(K)$. Compactness passes forward through continuous maps.

screens.title: The extreme value theorem
screens.prose: Let $f : K \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on a compact space $K \ne \varnothing$. `analysis` l17 proved the theorem on intervals by sequences; now it holds for any compact $K$.
screens.question: Prove that $f$ attains a maximum. Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $f(K)$ is compact, by the last screen.
So $f(K)$ is closed and bounded in $\mathbb{R}$, by Heine-Borel (l9).
Bounded and non-empty, it has a supremum $s$, by completeness.
Closed, it contains its supremum, a limit of its points: $s = f(c)$ for some $c \in K$. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Compact image, then Heine-Borel.
A closed bounded set of reals holds its supremum.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Start from the compactness of $f(K)$.

explain.text: The image is compact, hence closed and bounded. Its supremum exists and lies in it. So $f(c) = \max f$ for some $c$, on any compact $K$.

screens.title: Uniform continuity on a compact set
screens.prose: Let $f : K \to Y$ be continuous, $K$ a compact metric space, $\varepsilon > 0$. Each $x$ has $\delta_x$ with $f(B(x, \delta_x)) \subseteq B(f(x), \tfrac\varepsilon2)$. We want one $\delta$ for every $x$.
screens.question: Which step gives the single $\delta$?

options.text: The balls $B(x, \delta_x)$ cover $K$; take $\delta$ a Lebesgue number of this cover (l9).
Take $\delta = \min_x \delta_x$ over all $x \in K$.
options.why: There are infinitely many $\delta_x$, and their infimum may be 0. The Lebesgue number is the finite substitute.

options.text: Take $\delta = \delta_{x_0}$ for one fixed point $x_0$.
options.why: One point's $\delta$ can be far too large elsewhere, where $f$ is steep.

hints.text: The balls round each $x$ form an open cover.
Points closer than a Lebesgue number lie in one ball, so their images are within $\varepsilon$.

feedback.correct: Right. The Lebesgue number makes the choice uniform.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the cover by the balls $B(x, \delta_x)$.

explain.text: If $d(x, y) < \delta$, both lie in one ball $B(z, \delta_z)$. Then $f(x)$ and $f(y)$ are each within $\tfrac\varepsilon2$ of $f(z)$, so within $\varepsilon$ of each other.

screens.title: A uniform $\delta$ for $\sqrt x$
screens.prose: On $[0, 1]$, $|\sqrt x - \sqrt y| \le \sqrt{|x - y|}$ for all $x, y$. So one $\delta$ works everywhere, even at 0, where $\sqrt x$ is steepest.
screens.question: Give $\delta$ in terms of $\varepsilon$ so that $|x - y| < \delta$ forces $|\sqrt x - \sqrt y| < \varepsilon$.

hints.text: We need $\sqrt{|x - y|} < \varepsilon$.
Square both sides.

byKey.root: You took a root instead of squaring. $\sqrt{\sqrt\varepsilon}$ exceeds $\varepsilon$ for small $\varepsilon$.

explain.text: $|x - y| < \varepsilon^2$ gives $|\sqrt x - \sqrt y| \le \sqrt{|x - y|} < \varepsilon$. At $\varepsilon = 0.1$ that is $\delta = 0.01$. Near 0 no larger $\delta$ works.

screens.title: Compact onto Hausdorff
screens.prose: Let $h : K \to Y$ be a continuous bijection, $K$ compact and $Y$ Hausdorff. We show $h^{-1}$ is continuous: $h$ maps closed sets to closed sets.
screens.question: Put the proof in order.

lines.text: $F$ is compact, as a closed subset of a compact space (l9).
$h(F)$ is compact, as a continuous image of a compact set.
$h(F)$ is closed, since compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed.
So $(h^{-1})^{-1}(F) = h(F)$ is closed for every closed $F$: $h^{-1}$ is continuous. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Closed, then compact, then compact image, then closed.
The last step uses preimages under $h^{-1}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Such a bijection is a homeomorphism.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow a closed set $F$ through the chain.

explain.text: Closed in compact is compact, its image is compact, and compact in Hausdorff is closed. So $h$ sends closed sets to closed sets, which makes $h^{-1}$ continuous (l4).

screens.title: The circle, settled
screens.prose: In l7, $t \mapsto (\cos t, \sin t)$ from $[0, 2\pi)$ onto the circle was a continuous bijection without a continuous inverse. The circle is Hausdorff.
screens.question: Why does the last screen not apply?

options.text: $[0, 2\pi)$ is not compact, and on the compact $[0, 2\pi]$ the map is not one-to-one.
The circle is not Hausdorff.
options.why: The circle is a metric space, so it is Hausdorff.

options.text: The map is not continuous at $2\pi$.
options.why: $2\pi$ is not in $[0, 2\pi)$; on its domain the map is continuous.

hints.text: Check each hypothesis: compact, bijective, Hausdorff.
Adding $2\pi$ makes the domain compact but sends 0 and $2\pi$ to the same point.

feedback.correct: Right. One hypothesis fails either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test compactness of the domain.

explain.text: $[0, 2\pi)$ is not closed, so not compact. Closing it to $[0, 2\pi]$ restores compactness but loses one-to-one at $(1, 0)$. So the theorem never covered this map.

screens.title: Closed in, closed out?
screens.prose: A learner says: "Continuous maps send closed sets to closed sets." The hyperbola $xy = 1$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Project it by $(x, y) \mapsto x$.
screens.question: What is the image, and what does it show?

options.text: $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, not closed: continuous images of closed sets need not be closed
$\mathbb{R}$, which is closed, as the learner says
options.why: You assumed closed goes to closed. No point of $xy = 1$ has $x = 0$, so 0 is missed.

options.text: The projection is not continuous, so nothing follows
options.why: $(x, y) \mapsto x$ is continuous: $|x - x'| \le d_2$.

hints.text: Which $x$ values appear on the hyperbola?
Every $x \ne 0$, with $y = \tfrac1x$.
0 is a limit of the image but not in it.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the set of $x$ values on the curve.

byKey.claim: You carried closedness through the map. The image misses 0, a limit of its points.

explain.text: The projection is $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$, not closed; likewise $\arctan$ maps the closed $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(-\tfrac\pi2, \tfrac\pi2)$. Closedness is lost, while compactness is kept.

screens.title: The converse fails
screens.prose: The theorem says compact domains give compact images. Consider $f(x) = xe^{-x}$ on $[0, \infty)$, and $\sin$ on $\mathbb{R}$.
screens.question: Which statement is right?

options.text: Both images, $[0, \tfrac1e]$ and $[-1, 1]$, are compact, though the domains are not.
A compact image forces a compact domain.
options.why: You reversed the theorem. $\sin$ maps all of $\mathbb{R}$ onto the compact $[-1, 1]$.

options.text: $[0, \tfrac1e]$ cannot be compact, since $[0, \infty)$ is not.
options.why: $[0, \tfrac1e]$ is closed and bounded, so it is compact by Heine-Borel.

hints.text: Is $[0, \tfrac1e]$ closed and bounded?
The theorem has one direction only.

feedback.correct: Right. The implication runs one way.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Test each image with Heine-Borel.

explain.text: $f([0, \infty)) = [0, \tfrac1e]$, since $f \ge 0$, $f(1) = \tfrac1e$ is the peak and $f(0) = 0$. $\sin(\mathbb{R}) = [-1, 1]$. Both are compact; the domains are not.

screens.title: A minimum-risk portfolio exists
screens.prose: Two assets have volatilities 20% and 10%, correlation 0.3. Long-only weights $w_1 \in [0, 1]$ form a compact set, and volatility is continuous. So a minimum-volatility long-only portfolio exists.
screens.question: What weight $w_1$ on the 20% asset minimises volatility? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: $w_1 = \tfrac{\sigma_2^2 - \rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Set the derivative of the variance to 0.

byKey.norho: 0.2 is $\tfrac{0.01}{0.05}$, which ignores the correlation term.
byKey.other: 0.8947 is the weight on the 10% asset. The question asks for the 20% asset.

explain.text: $w_1 = \tfrac{0.004}{0.038} \approx 0.1053$, with volatility about 9.787%, below either asset alone. Compactness promised a minimum; calculus found it.

screens.title: A minimum on the edge
screens.prose: Raise the correlation to 0.6. The unconstrained minimum is now at $w_1 = \tfrac{0.01 - 0.012}{0.026} \approx -0.0769$, a short position in the riskier asset.
screens.question: Where is the long-only minimum?

options.text: At the edge $w_1 = 0$: all in the 10% asset, volatility 10%
There is none, since the true minimum is outside $[0, 1]$
options.why: $[0, 1]$ is compact and volatility continuous, so a minimum on it exists. It moves to the edge.

options.text: At $w_1 \approx -0.0769$
options.why: That weight is short, outside the long-only set.

hints.text: On $[0, 1]$ the curve only rises from $w_1 = 0$.
The minimum over $[0, 1]$ sits at its end.

feedback.correct: Right. Compactness promises a minimum, not an interior one.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Follow the solid part of the curve.

explain.text: On $[0, 1]$ the volatility increases from 10% at $w_1 = 0$. So the long-only minimum is the edge point. Compactness guarantees existence, not that the answer is inside.

ideas: A continuous image of a compact set is compact. Pull an open cover back, take a finite subcover, push it forward.
So a continuous real function on a non-empty compact set attains its extremes. It is uniformly continuous, by a Lebesgue number. A continuous bijection from compact onto Hausdorff is a homeomorphism.
Closedness is not kept ($xy = 1$ projects onto $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$), and the converse fails ($\sin(\mathbb{R}) = [-1, 1]$).

formula.name: Compact images
formula.tex: K \text{ compact}, \ f \text{ continuous} \implies f(K) \text{ compact}
formula.note: Pull the cover back with $f^{-1}$; images of open sets are never used.

summary.trap: Continuous maps need not send closed sets to closed sets: the hyperbola $xy = 1$ projects onto $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}$.

quiz.prose: For $\sqrt x$ on $[0, 1]$ the uniform choice is $\delta = \varepsilon^2$.
quiz.question: What is $\delta$ for $\varepsilon = 0.1$?

byKey.root: You took the root. The uniform $\delta$ is the square.

explain.text: $\delta = 0.1^2 = 0.01$. Points within 0.01 have square roots within 0.1, at 0 as anywhere.

Any continuous $f$ on $(0, 1)$
